paragraphs: Differentiable simulators let reinforcement learning algorithms calculate how changes in actions affect simulated outcomes. These gradients can have lower variance than the estimates used by model-free approaches. Physical contact creates a difficulty, however: stiff dynamics can introduce sampling error into the gradients. The paper investigates this source of error in learning control policies.

The proposed Adaptive Horizon Actor-Critic, or AHAC, changes how far the algorithm follows the differentiable model when calculating its update. It adapts this model-based horizon to avoid stiff dynamics. The approach therefore makes the length of the gradient calculation responsive to the behavior of the simulation, reducing the gradient error associated with those difficult regions.

Across the reported locomotion tasks, AHAC achieves 40% more reward than the model-free reinforcement learning baselines. The authors also report improved efficiency in elapsed training time and effective scaling to high-dimensional control environments. These findings support adaptive horizons as a useful way to obtain the benefits of differentiable simulation in the contact-rich tasks studied.
icml-2024-adaptive-horizon-actor-critic-.tldr: AHAC adapts the differentiable simulation horizon to reduce gradient errors around stiff dynamics and improve control learning.

paragraphs: A transformer might solve a task from examples in its input by internally carrying out an iterative learning algorithm. Showing that its architecture can represent such an algorithm leaves an important question unanswered: can training actually find that solution? This paper addresses that learning question for in-context linear regression using linear looped transformers, whose layers share weights.

The authors show that the global minimizer of the population training loss performs multiple steps of preconditioned gradient descent. The preconditioner adapts to the data distribution, so the learned procedure adjusts the geometry of its updates to the regression problems it encounters. This connects the best solution to an identifiable iterative algorithm.

They also prove fast convergence for gradient flow on the regression loss, despite its nonconvex landscape, using a gradient dominance condition. Synthetic experiments support the theoretical findings. The contribution is a learnability result for the specified linear, weight-sharing setting: it explains both the algorithm implemented by an optimum and how the analyzed training dynamics can converge.
icml-2024-can-looped-transformers-learn-.tldr: For in-context linear regression, linear looped transformers have an optimal solution that implements multi-step preconditioned gradient descent, with a fast gradient-flow convergence guarantee.

paragraphs: Customer churn analysis can ask how an intervention changes whether customers leave, rather than only predicting their departure. This paper uses the potential outcomes framework to study those intervention effects. Its tensorized latent factor block hazard model brings customer characteristics, time, and intervention structure into a common representation for causal analysis.

A central component is 1-bit tensor completion, which estimates the model's parameter tensor from binary churn records. The formulation captures hidden customer characteristics and temporal effects while accommodating the binary observations and their time-monotonic behavior. The model also groups interventions according to similar impacts, making the estimated effects more useful for organizing customer retention strategies.

For computation, the authors combine projected gradient descent with spectral clustering. They establish theoretical properties that apply at finite sample sizes, rather than relying only on limiting behavior as data grows. Experiments on simulated and real-world applications report advantages for the proposed model. Together, these contributions connect structured causal modeling with an algorithm intended to make intervention analysis practical.
icml-2024-causal-customer-churn-analysis.tldr: A tensor-based causal churn model captures hidden customer and time effects while grouping interventions by their impact.

paragraphs: Actor-critic algorithms combine a policy-learning actor with a critic that estimates its performance. Their theoretical analyses often leave out features used in practical implementations. This paper organizes five such features into a joint target: multilayer neural networks for both components, Markovian sampling, continuous state and action spaces, guarantees for the final iterate, and global optimality.

Addressing these features together matters because they describe different parts of the same learning process. Markovian samples account for dependence along interactions with an environment. A last-iterate guarantee concerns the policy obtained at the end of training. Neural network parameterization and continuous spaces bring the analyzed setting closer to common actor-critic implementations.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis covering all five criteria and establish a global convergence sample complexity bound of approximately epsilon to the power of minus three, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Their argument uses a weak gradient domination property of Markov decision processes and an analysis of critic estimation error. The result links the quality of critic estimates to a global guarantee for the final policy.
icml-2024-closing-the-gap-achieving-glob.tldr: The paper establishes last-iterate global convergence bounds for actor-critic learning while jointly accounting for five practically relevant features.

paragraphs: In long-tailed classification, some classes have many training examples while others have few. This imbalance makes it difficult to obtain the neural collapse structure often observed in well-trained networks on balanced data. The paper treats that representational structure as a useful target for improving learning when class frequencies are uneven.

The proposed Distribution Alignment Optimization loss, called DisA, approaches the problem through distribution matching. It encourages the distribution of representations in the network's last layer to align with an ideal equiangular tight frame, or ETF, structure. This gives training an explicit target for the overall arrangement of its learned representations.

DisA is designed as an additional loss that can be combined with most existing methods for long-tailed learning. The authors develop versions for both fixed classifiers and classifiers learned during training, covering two ways of organizing the final prediction stage. Extensive experiments support the method's effectiveness. The stated contribution is a broadly combinable way to encourage a desirable representation geometry under class imbalance.
icml-2024-distribution-alignment-optimiz.tldr: DisA improves long-tailed classification by aligning final-layer representations with an ideal neural collapse structure.

paragraphs: Feature visualization creates patterns that strongly activate parts of a neural network, with the aim of explaining what those parts detect. This paper investigates whether the resulting images reliably describe how a network processes natural inputs. Its central concern is the connection between an optimized visualization and the behavior that visualization is supposed to explain.

The authors first construct network circuits that make feature visualization display arbitrary patterns unrelated to normal behavior on natural images. They then provide evidence of a related phenomenon in ordinary, unmodified networks: optimized visualizations are processed very differently from standard inputs. Comparing those processing behaviors offers a sanity check for interpretations based on the generated images.

The theoretical analysis shows that the class of functions reliably understandable through feature visualization is extremely restricted and excludes general black-box neural networks. These findings challenge the assumption that a compelling visualization is sufficient evidence of a feature's natural role. The authors suggest that imposing suitable structure on networks could be a promising route toward more reliable visual explanations.
icml-2024-dont-trust-your-eyes-on-the-un.tldr: Feature visualizations can be disconnected from natural-input behavior, and the paper identifies empirical and theoretical reasons to question their reliability.

paragraphs: An agent's ability to generalize depends partly on which environments it experiences during training. This paper studies how selecting or generating individual levels affects zero-shot transfer. It considers both adaptive sampling of available levels and unsupervised environment design, where the training procedure can create levels itself.

For deep actor-critic models with shared base layers, the authors show that prioritizing levels by value loss minimizes mutual information between the agent's internal representation and the training-level set in the generated data. This gives a theoretical explanation for the regularization produced by certain sampling strategies. They also find that existing environment-design methods can shift the training distribution substantially, with poor zero-shot generalization.

Data-Regularised Environment Design, or DRED, addresses both overfitting and distribution shift by grounding level generation in an initial set of level parameters. A generative model learns to approximate their underlying distribution and produces new levels from that grounding. The authors report significant zero-shot generalization improvements over adaptive sampling strategies and existing environment-design methods, supporting distribution-aware generation as a useful training approach.
icml-2024-dred-zero-shot-transfer-in-rei.tldr: DRED improves zero-shot reinforcement learning transfer by generating training levels from a model grounded in an initial level distribution.

paragraphs: Equivariance means that transforming an input produces a corresponding transformation of a model's prediction. This paper studies how that property can arise in the collective prediction of a deep ensemble trained with data augmentation. Its focus is the symmetry of the combined output, even when individual ensemble members do not exhibit that symmetry.

Using neural tangent kernel theory, the authors establish equivariance in the infinite-width limit for any architecture. The result applies at every training time and to all inputs, including inputs outside the data manifold. That scope matters: the theoretical property extends beyond the kinds of examples represented by the training data and does not require waiting until training has finished.

The equivariance is therefore emergent at the ensemble level. Predictions from individually nonequivariant members combine into an equivariant prediction under the analyzed limit. Detailed numerical experiments verify the theoretical insights. The paper connects data augmentation, collective prediction, and symmetry through a formal result whose stated infinite-width condition is essential to understanding the guarantee.
icml-2024-emergent-equivariance-in-deep-.tldr: In the infinite-width limit, data augmentation makes deep ensembles equivariant for all inputs and training times, even when individual members are not.

paragraphs: A vision-and-language navigation agent must interpret an instruction and choose a sequence of actions that reaches its target. When instructions arrive online, the agent can use unlabeled test examples to adapt as it operates. The difficulty is choosing how to update a model while both successive instructions and the steps within each instruction unfold.

Frequent updates can cause large changes in the model's parameters, while infrequent updates can leave it poorly prepared for changing environments. Fast-Slow Test-Time Adaptation, or FSTTA, addresses this tension through a unified analysis of gradients and parameters. Its approach jointly uses decomposition and accumulation, treating the update information and the model state together.

This framing makes adaptation responsive to the two levels of navigation activity: executing instructions over time and deciding multiple actions within each execution. The authors evaluate the method on four benchmarks and report substantial performance gains. Those results support the proposed fast-slow approach for improving online navigation through unlabeled test-time experience.
icml-2024-fast-slow-test-time-adaptation.tldr: FSTTA jointly analyzes gradients and parameters to improve online navigation adaptation while addressing the tension between frequent and infrequent updates.

paragraphs: In a bandit problem, a learner repeatedly selects among options called arms. This paper introduces a setting where selecting one arm can also change the expected rewards of other arms. A graph specifies these relationships: an edge means that pulling either connected arm triggers the evolution of the other.

The model includes rested and restless bandits as special graph configurations while allowing more general dependencies. The authors first study optimal decision-making when the graph has no prescribed structure and show that computing an optimal policy is NP-hard. For graphs composed of fully connected groups, however, they derive an optimal policy in closed form.

They then develop learning algorithms for both deterministic and stochastic cases. Their regret bounds include terms reflecting properties of the particular graph, showing how interaction structure contributes to learning difficulty. The paper also shows that knowing the underlying graph is not necessary for achieving no regret. Together, these results distinguish the computational challenge of planning from the statistical challenge of learning in interconnected bandit systems.
icml-2024-graph-triggered-rising-bandits.tldr: Graph-triggered bandits model actions that change connected options, with planning and learning guarantees that depend on graph structure.

paragraphs: Energy-based models describe data through an energy function that defines an unnormalized probability density. They offer flexibility but are difficult to train. Adversarial energy-based models add a generator and use a minimax training game to avoid the expensive Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling of traditional approaches, yet their generation quality still trails stronger generative models.

This paper brings a diffusion process into that adversarial framework. It places energy-based models within individual denoising steps, dividing a long generation process into several smaller stages. The training method also uses a symmetric Jeffrey divergence and a variational posterior distribution for the generator to address challenges in adversarial energy-based learning.

Experiments show significant improvements in generation relative to existing adversarial energy-based models. The resulting model also provides an energy function useful for efficient density estimation. The contribution therefore concerns two connected objectives: improving the samples produced by the generator and retaining the density-modeling functionality that motivates energy-based approaches in the first place.
icml-2024-improving-adversarial-energy-b.tldr: Embedding adversarial energy-based models into diffusion denoising steps improves generation while retaining a useful energy function for density estimation.

paragraphs: Learning problems involving three-dimensional rotations require a choice about how those rotations are represented. Several representations are available, and selecting one can be difficult because their properties interact with the learning process. This paper serves as a survey and practical guide to making that choice for models trained with gradient-based optimization.

The authors consolidate insights from rotation-based learning and organize them around properties that can help or hinder optimization. Their subject is learning functions that involve rotations, so the role of the representation extends beyond simply recording an orientation. The guide connects representation properties to the conditions under which a model must learn from or predict rotations.

Its recommendations distinguish between rotations supplied as model inputs and rotations produced as model outputs. They also account for whether the data primarily contains small angles. These distinctions make the guidance conditional on the task and data. The paper's contribution is a consolidated basis for choosing a suitable representation, with attention to the specific way rotations enter the learning problem.
icml-2024-learning-with-3d-rotations-a-h.tldr: This survey guides rotation-representation choices according to their optimization properties, their input or output role, and whether angles are mostly small.

paragraphs: Music understanding requires handling structure that presents challenges beyond those of other audio tasks. LLark is an instruction-tuned multimodal model designed to respond to requests about music. It combines a pretrained generative music model with a pretrained language model, bringing music-focused modeling and text generation into one architecture.

The authors also develop a dataset creation process. They augment annotations from diverse open-source music datasets and convert the resulting material into a shared instruction-tuning format. This common format makes differently annotated music collections usable within the same training approach. Both the music data and the models used for training come entirely from open-source resources.

Evaluation covers music understanding, captioning, and reasoning. LLark matches or exceeds existing baselines on understanding tasks, while human evaluations show strong agreement with its captioning and reasoning responses. These are distinct forms of evidence for its capabilities: comparative task performance and human agreement with generated answers. The authors also release training code, making the construction process available alongside the model's reported results.
icml-2024-llark-a-multimodal-instruction.tldr: LLark combines pretrained music and language models with unified instruction data to support music understanding, captioning, and reasoning.

paragraphs: Masks obscure facial information and can make face representations incomplete or inaccurate. This paper proposes a unified network that transfers information from a generative task into identity recognition. It trains three modules in sequence using synthetic masked faces, giving each stage a distinct role in handling occlusion and distinguishing identities.

First, an encoder pretrained for face inpainting is fine-tuned to produce category-aware descriptors of masked faces. Its ability to recover contextual information supports representations that are robust to different masks. A multilayer convolutional module then converts those descriptors into identity-aware vectors. This conversion is supervised by distilling relational knowledge from an existing face recognition model.

The encoder and conversion module together form the pretrained backbone. A final classifier, consisting of a fully connected layer followed by a softmax layer, is fine-tuned to identify the resulting vectors. Experiments on synthetic and realistic datasets demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The central idea is to connect contextual recovery with identity discrimination through an explicitly staged representation-learning process.
icml-2024-masked-face-recognition-with-g.tldr: The method turns representations learned for face inpainting into identity-aware features to improve masked face recognition.

paragraphs: Neural networks can memorize training examples, including datasets with random labels. This paper proposes measuring memorization at the level of individual samples using the curvature of the loss function around each example. Averaging that curvature over training epochs produces a score that reflects the sample's behavior throughout learning.

The authors test whether this score captures known memorization patterns on popular image datasets. They report both qualitative and quantitative agreement, including validation against previously released memorization scores. This connects a property of the local loss geometry to an independently measured tendency to memorize particular examples.

Experiments also show that corrupted labels are learned with high curvature, and curvature-based detection outperforms existing approaches for finding mislabeled examples. Qualitative inspection associates high-curvature samples with rare, mislabeled, or conflicting instances, indicating a likelihood of memorization rather than making every such sample a definitive case. The analysis additionally uncovers duplicated images carrying different labels in CIFAR100 and ImageNet, linking the proposed measure to a concrete dataset problem.
icml-2024-memorization-through-the-lens-.tldr: Average loss curvature around training samples provides an empirical signal of memorization and helps identify mislabeled or conflicting images.

paragraphs: Principal component regression combines principal component analysis with linear regression. This paper studies its generalization when high-dimensional observations have an underlying low-dimensional structure. The analysis assumes data sampled from a spiked covariance model, providing a specific setting in which to examine how representation choice affects prediction risk.

Using random matrix theory, the authors derive asymptotic guarantees for generalization risk in high dimensions. They also analyze distribution shift between training and test data. These results separate the effects of parameter count, the data-generating model, and model misspecification, helping clarify why changes in model size alone do not fully explain prediction performance.

In the analyzed setting, principal component regression acts as a regularizer and prevents the interpolation peak associated with double descent. This connects the absence of that peak to the use of principal components under the stated data model. Simulations validate the theoretical findings, supporting their relevance to the modeled conditions and showing how the predicted behavior appears in empirical experiments.
icml-2024-no-double-descent-in-principal.tldr: Under a spiked covariance data model, principal component regression regularizes learning and prevents the interpolation peak of double descent.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a foundation model can require storing a separate weight update for each customization. LoRA compresses those updates into products of low-rank matrices, but storage remains a concern when models or collections of customizations grow. This paper proposes FourierFT as another way to represent a weight update using very few trainable values.

FourierFT treats the update as a matrix in the spatial domain and learns only a small subset of its Fourier coefficients. An inverse discrete Fourier transform reconstructs the weight-update matrix from those trained coefficients. The trainable representation therefore lives in the spectral domain, while the recovered matrix supplies the change applied to the model's weights.

Experiments cover natural language understanding, generation, instruction tuning, and image classification. Across these tasks, FourierFT achieves comparable or better performance than LoRA with fewer parameters. In the reported LLaMA2-7B instruction-tuning example, it surpasses LoRA using 0.064 million trainable parameters versus 33.5 million. This illustrates the substantial compression that the spectral representation achieves in that evaluated setting.
icml-2024-parameter-efficient-fine-tunin.tldr: FourierFT learns a small subset of Fourier coefficients to represent weight updates, matching or beating LoRA with fewer trainable parameters in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Language models contain internal representations that are difficult for people to interpret directly. Patchscopes proposes using a language model's own ability to generate understandable text to explain those representations. The framework aims to answer different questions about the computations inside a model through natural-language inspection.

The authors show that many earlier techniques fit within this common framework. These include methods that project hidden representations into vocabulary space and methods that intervene in a model's computation. Bringing them together provides a shared way to understand their operation. Patchscopes can also mitigate shortcomings such as limited expressiveness and difficulty inspecting representations in early layers.

The framework enables additional uses, including having a more capable model explain the internal representations of a smaller one. The authors also demonstrate possibilities for correcting errors in multihop reasoning. Its contribution therefore spans both interpretation and intervention: it organizes existing inspection methods while expanding the kinds of representations and computational problems that can be examined.
icml-2024-patchscopes-a-unifying-framewo.tldr: Patchscopes uses language models to explain hidden representations in text while unifying and extending earlier interpretability methods.

paragraphs: This position paper argues for a general mathematical framework that connects two parts of neural network design: specifying constraints a model should satisfy and specifying an implementation. The authors contend that existing attempts do not provide a coherent bridge between those activities. Their proposal uses category theory to place both within one algebraic language.

More precisely, the proposed foundation is the universal algebra of monads valued in a 2-category of parametric maps. This formalism is intended to express both requirements on models and the structures used to build them. The ambition is a shared theory through which architecture constraints and concrete implementations can be studied together.

To support the position, the authors show how the theory recovers constraints from geometric deep learning and implementations of varied neural architectures, including recurrent neural networks. They also illustrate its ability to encode standard constructs from computer science and automata theory. These examples provide the paper's case for the framework's breadth; the contribution is a proposed unifying perspective supported by mathematical constructions.
icml-2024-position-categorical-deep-lear.tldr: This position paper proposes category theory as a common algebraic language for neural network constraints and implementations.

paragraphs: This paper studies online decisions subject to two kinds of constraints. Every action must belong to a fixed feasible set, while additional adversarially changing constraints need only be approximately satisfied on average. Because projecting onto the fixed set can be difficult, the algorithms access it through an oracle that minimizes linear objectives.

The first algorithm uses T linear-oracle calls over T rounds. Suppressing quantities other than T, it guarantees regret of order T^(3/4), up to logarithmic factors, and constraint violation of order T^(7/8). These bounds apply to any interval of the sequence. The algorithm additionally needs an oracle for minimizing a strongly convex nonsmooth function over a Euclidean ball.

A more efficient version removes that extra optimization oracle and uses only first-order access to the changing constraints. It obtains similar bounds for the complete sequence, rather than the interval guarantee stated for the first method. An extension to bandit feedback achieves similar dependence on T in expectation. The results make explicit the tradeoff between oracle requirements and the scope of the guarantees.
icml-2024-projection-free-online-convex-.tldr: The paper develops projection-free online algorithms with sublinear regret and constraint violation, trading stronger interval guarantees for additional oracle requirements.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent can learn visual features that work in its training domain but transfer poorly to unfamiliar appearances. This paper attributes part of that problem to the lack of explicit semantic constraints on the feature extractor. Prompt-based Visual Alignment, or PVA, introduces such constraints to support zero-shot policy transfer with limited cross-domain data.

PVA uses a vision-language model to connect images with semantic information expressed through text. That information supervises a visual aligner, which maps images from different domains into a unified domain. Prompt tuning learns a sequence of tokens to better express the semantic information used for alignment.

The aim is to give the agent a representation that remains useful across domains despite differences in visual appearance. The authors evaluate PVA on a vision-based autonomous driving task in the CARLA simulator. Their experiments show good generalization to unseen domains under limited access to data from multiple domains. This supports semantic alignment as a practical mechanism for transfer in the evaluated driving setting.
icml-2024-prompt-based-visual-alignment-.tldr: PVA uses learned text prompts and a vision-language model to align visual domains and improve zero-shot policy transfer with limited cross-domain data.

paragraphs: Macro placement is an important optimization step in chip design. Reinforcement learning has shown promise for improving placement quality, but existing approaches can require many online rollouts or substantial offline expert data to get started. Those demands motivate a method that uses its learning experience more efficiently.

EfficientPlace combines a global tree search with an agent that learns local policies. The search directs the overall optimization process, while the reinforcement learning component helps advance the search through local policy learning. This division gives the method a global mechanism for organizing exploration and a learned mechanism for making progress within that organization.

The authors evaluate the framework on commonly used benchmarks and report strong placement quality within a short time, outperforming recent leading approaches. The findings support integrating search and reinforcement learning as a route to faster, more sample-efficient macro placement. The paper's central contribution is the interaction between the global search procedure and the locally trained agent, aimed at reducing the experience burden of placement optimization.
icml-2024-reinforcement-learning-within-.tldr: EfficientPlace combines global tree search with local reinforcement learning to achieve strong macro placement quality in a short time.

paragraphs: Exploiting an opponent's weaknesses can make a game-playing strategy vulnerable, especially when the opponent model is inaccurate or the opponent is deceptive. This paper introduces adaptation safety as a way to define the acceptable risk of exploitation. Its starting point is that computationally limited strategies may already be exploitable before any opponent-specific adaptation.

Adaptation safety requires that exploiting the opponent should not make a strategy more exploitable than it would have been without that adaptation. The reference point is therefore the strategy's existing vulnerability. This definition makes the safety requirement directly about the additional risk introduced by trying to take advantage of an opponent.

The authors build Opponent eXploitation Search, or OX-Search, around this principle, incorporating real-time search for efficient online exploitation. Their theoretical analysis establishes adaptation safety and robust exploitation even with inaccurate opponent models. Evaluations in poker games show improvements over earlier methods in both exploitation and exploitability. Together, the definition and algorithm connect opponent-specific gains to an explicit bound on added strategic vulnerability.
icml-2024-safe-and-robust-subgame-exploi.tldr: OX-Search exploits opponents while satisfying adaptation safety: exploitation should not increase vulnerability relative to the strategy without adaptation.

paragraphs: Flat regions of a neural network's loss landscape are often associated with simple learned models, but the connection requires explanation. This paper studies that relationship for a class of two-layer networks. It asks how minimizing sharpness shapes the features learned by stochastic gradient descent with label noise.

For high-dimensional training data, certain activation functions, and a sufficiently small step size, the authors show that label-noise SGD converges to a network whose neurons repeat one linear feature. The resulting feature matrix has rank one. Under these stated conditions, simplicity is therefore expressed as a precise structural property of the learned representation.

The main technical result shows that label-noise SGD minimizes sharpness on the manifold of zero-loss models for the studied two-layer networks. The proof identifies a local geodesic convexity property of the loss Hessian's trace near approximate stationary points on that manifold. This connects sharpness to the geometry of zero-loss solutions and supplies a route from the training dynamics to the rank-one conclusion.
icml-2024-simplicity-bias-via-global-con.tldr: For a specified class of two-layer networks and sufficiently small steps, label-noise SGD minimizes sharpness and converges to rank-one linear features.

paragraphs: Backpropagation can make language-model fine-tuning expensive in memory. Zeroth-order optimization estimates gradients using forward passes, offering a more memory-efficient route. This paper combines that approach with variance reduction to improve the stability and convergence of fine-tuning updates, introducing Memory-Efficient Zeroth-Order Stochastic Variance-Reduced Gradient, or MeZO-SVRG.

The method is evaluated on GLUE tasks using both masked and autoregressive language models. It outperforms MeZO in full-parameter and partial-parameter fine-tuning, with reported test-accuracy increases of up to 20%. The authors also report effectiveness without relying on task-specific prompts, addressing a dependency described for the earlier MeZO approach.

The benefits extend to resource use in the experiments. MeZO-SVRG often exceeds MeZO's peak test accuracy using half the GPU-hours. Compared with first-order SGD, it uses half the memory for autoregressive models, and its relative memory savings improve as batch sizes grow. These findings support variance reduction as a way to make forward-pass-based fine-tuning more effective while preserving its memory advantage.
icml-2024-variance-reduced-zeroth-order-.tldr: MeZO-SVRG adds variance reduction to forward-pass-based fine-tuning, improving reported accuracy and efficiency while retaining substantial memory savings.
